title: Three Courts, Three Answers, One Fee — The H-1B Circuit Split Heading to the Supreme Court
excerpt: A Boston judge struck down the $100,000 fee. A Washington judge upheld it. A San Francisco case is pending. The contradiction all but guarantees the Supreme Court will decide.
body:
Three federal judges. Three different courts. Three different answers to the same question: can a president slap a $100,000 fee on an H-1B visa?

On June 8, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston vacated Trump's fee in its entirety, calling it an unconstitutional tax that only Congress can levy. Five months earlier, Judge Beryl Howell in Washington, D.C. upheld the exact same fee, ruling that the president acted within his immigration authority. And in San Francisco, a third lawsuit — filed by religious organisations and labour groups — is still pending before a court in the Ninth Circuit.

The result is a textbook circuit split, the kind of legal contradiction that all but guarantees the Supreme Court will eventually have to weigh in. For the roughly 344,000 people who filed H-1B petitions this year — more than 70 per cent of them Indian nationals — the question of which court's ruling controls is not academic. It determines whether their employer owes $5,000 or $100,000.

## Two judges, opposite conclusions

Judge Howell, an Obama appointee sitting in D.C., ruled in December 2025 that the $100,000 payment was a lawful exercise of presidential authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce had challenged the fee; Howell rejected their arguments. That case is now on appeal before the D.C. Circuit.

Judge Sorokin, also an Obama appointee but sitting in Boston, reached the opposite conclusion. His 42-page ruling found that the fee was a tax — not a penalty, not a restriction, not a regulatory charge. And because only Congress has the constitutional power to levy taxes, Trump's proclamation "did not carry the force of law."

Sorokin's reasoning leaned heavily on the Supreme Court's February 2026 decision striking down Trump's emergency tariffs. In that case, the justices held that sweeping import duties imposed under a national emergency law were, in substance, taxes that the president lacked authority to impose. Sorokin applied the same logic: if tariffs on goods are a tax requiring congressional authorisation, so is a $100,000 charge on visa petitions.

The White House has said it will appeal, and expressed confidence the ruling will be reversed. Spokesperson Taylor Rogers noted that "a federal judge in Washington already upheld a nearly identical order."

That is precisely the problem. When two federal judges look at the same executive action and reach opposite conclusions, the appellate courts must resolve the conflict. And when two different circuit courts disagree, the Supreme Court steps in.

## The San Francisco wild card

A third lawsuit, filed in the Northern District of California by religious groups and labour organisations, adds another variable. If the Ninth Circuit — historically the most sceptical of executive overreach — rules against the fee, that would create a three-circuit split: the First Circuit (Boston) striking it down, the D.C. Circuit potentially upholding it, and the Ninth Circuit weighing in from the West Coast.

Three circuits in conflict would make Supreme Court review nearly certain.

## The eighty-five who already paid

While the courts sort out the legal theory, 85 employers have already paid the $100,000 fee, sending a combined $8.5 million to USCIS. Judge Sorokin's ruling vacated the policy, but neither his decision nor the administration's response has addressed what happens to that money.

If the fee is ultimately ruled unlawful, those employers would presumably be entitled to refunds. But refund mechanisms for vacated agency policies are notoriously slow and uncertain. If the D.C. Circuit upholds the fee on appeal before the First Circuit rules, the legal landscape becomes even murkier — with the fee simultaneously valid in one jurisdiction and void in another.

For employers considering whether to sponsor new H-1B workers, the uncertainty is paralysing. A petition filed today could be subject to the $100,000 fee or exempt from it, depending on which circuit's ruling controls.

## What the tariff precedent means for immigration law

Sorokin's use of the Supreme Court's tariff ruling is the most consequential legal development in this saga. The tariff decision established a broad principle: the executive branch cannot impose financial charges that function as taxes, regardless of what label the administration puts on them.

If that reasoning holds on appeal, it would constrain not just the $100,000 H-1B fee but any future attempt by a president to impose substantial financial charges on visa applications through executive action. Congress, not the White House, would set the price of immigration.

The administration has a counterargument: immigration law gives the president broad authority to "restrict the entry" of foreign nationals deemed detrimental to American interests. A $100,000 charge, they argue, is a restriction, not a tax. But Sorokin rejected that framing outright: "Taxes are not 'restrictions,'" he wrote.

## The timeline ahead

The appeals will take months. The D.C. Circuit will likely hear arguments on the Chamber of Commerce case before the end of 2026. The First Circuit will hear the government's appeal of Sorokin's ruling on a similar timeline. The San Francisco case could move faster or slower depending on judicial scheduling.

The $100,000 fee was originally set to expire on September 21, 2026, one year after Trump's proclamation. But with Congress now pushing the PROTECT Act to codify the fee permanently and the courts still fighting over its legality, the September expiration may be rendered moot by legislation before the judiciary finishes its work.

For Indian H-1B workers and their employers, the practical advice has not changed: budget for uncertainty. The fee may be dead in Boston, alive in Washington, and undecided in San Francisco. Until the Supreme Court speaks — or Congress acts — nobody knows what the H-1B programme costs.
